historical_timeline.summary: Sworn in as U.S. senator from Massachusetts, the first African American elected to the Senate by popular vote.
Discomfort in the right breast; mammogram, sonogram, and needle biopsy show breast cancer.
Operation for breast cancer (reported as a double mastectomy) with removal of the right-sided lymph nodes.
Begins speaking publicly about breast cancer in men.
Died at his home in Coral Gables, Florida, aged 95.

claims.statement: Edward William Brooke III was born in Washington, D.C., on October 26, 1919.

source_links.locator: Interview: 'I'm 83, I will be 84 on October 26th'

claims.statement: Brooke was elected attorney general of Massachusetts in 1962 and re-elected in 1964, and in 1966 became the first African American elected to the U.S. Senate by popular vote; he served as a Republican senator from Massachusetts from January 3, 1967, to January 3, 1979.

In a CNN interview aired on June 11, 2003, Brooke said that in September 2002 he felt discomfort in his right breast, which he dismissed as aging, possible muscle strain, or gas; that he then had a mammogram, a sonogram, and a needle biopsy, which found a malignant tumor; that his breasts had never before been examined by a doctor; and that he had not thought men got breast cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public account of the delay before seeking care, which the synthetic episode uses as a teaching point. No other detail of his diagnosis is used.

claims.statement: In the same interview Brooke said he had to be operated on for breast cancer, that the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, and that all of the lymph nodes on his right side were removed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Nodal involvement and an axillary dissection as he described them; the number of nodes was not made public.

claims.statement: An Associated Press report of June 11, 2003, said that Brooke, 83, had been diagnosed with breast cancer in September, had a double mastectomy, and was free of the cancer, and that he was encouraging men to examine themselves and urging insurers to cover mammograms for men.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The only fetched source that names the operation. The CNN interview does not contradict it.

source_links.locator: Breast cancer section; diagnosis in September 2002
Title-level record of the June 10, 2003, interview; the article itself was not read

claims.statement: Brooke said he kept the diagnosis private for several months and then, in June 2003, began speaking publicly about breast cancer in men, saying 'Men have breast tissue like women, and they can have breast cancer, and they do,' and urging men 'not to be so macho about this whole thing'; he called for national awareness, early detection, and insurance coverage of mammograms for men.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The destigmatization message at the center of the record.

claims.statement: In the 2003 interview Brooke described himself as not a smoker or a drinker and said he exercised and ate fairly good food.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public description, used for the social history.

claims.statement: Brooke died at his home in Coral Gables, Florida, on January 3, 2015, aged 95; his former chief counsel said he died of natural causes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; no further detail of his last years is used.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Men get breast cancer. Care for a man of 83 with node-positive, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer after bilateral mastectomy, on the ASCO male breast cancer guideline and the NCCN breast guideline: tamoxifen as the preferred adjuvant endocrine therapy for men (not an aromatase inhibitor alone), with venous thromboembolism, mood, hot flash, sexual side effect, and adherence checks at every visit; germline genetic testing and genetic counseling offered to every man with breast cancer, with information for relatives; bone health on hormone therapy at his age; and survivorship care with no routine imaging or tumor markers. His own public account, that he dismissed his symptoms and had never had his chest examined, frames the teaching on why men present late.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week follow-up on tamoxifen; bone density results; medical oncology seen today

hpi.narrative: Mr. Brooke returns four weeks after his first visit. He has taken tamoxifen 20 mg every day for fifteen weeks and keeps the bottle by his toothbrush. He has mild hot flashes two or three times a week, mostly at night, which do not stop him sleeping. He has had no leg swelling or pain, chest pain, or breathlessness, and no change in vision. The mastectomy scars are comfortable and he has full movement of the right shoulder, with no arm swelling. He had his DXA scan this morning and saw Dr. Cho of medical oncology, who has taken over his tamoxifen and sent a germline genetic test today. He starts vitamin D today for the low level found at the first visit. He walks most days.

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-month follow-up on tamoxifen; germline result

hpi.narrative: Mr. Brooke returns three months after his last visit, about six and a half months into tamoxifen. He has missed no doses; his pill organizer is empty on the right days. Hot flashes are unchanged, mild, two or three times a week. Asked today about sexual side effects, which were not covered at the last visit, he says his libido has been lower since starting tamoxifen; erections are adequate, and he is not troubled enough to want treatment. He has had no leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness, or change in vision, and no new lump or swelling on the chest wall or in either armpit. He met the genetic counselor four weeks ago: the multigene panel found no pathogenic variant in BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, or the other genes tested, and he was given a letter to share with his relatives. He takes vitamin D daily and walks most days.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Brooke returns three months after his last visit, about nine and a half months into tamoxifen and ten months after surgery. He has missed no doses. Hot flashes remain mild; libido is unchanged and he is not troubled by it. He has had no leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness, or change in vision, and no new lump, skin change, or swelling on either side of the chest or in either armpit, no bone pain, cough, or weight loss. Since his last visit he has begun speaking publicly about breast cancer in men, to encourage men to have a lump or discomfort in the chest checked and to ask their doctors to examine them. He walks most days and feels well.

referral.pertinent_history: He noticed discomfort in the right breast and at first put it down to aging or a strained muscle; he had never had a chest examination by a doctor. Mammography and ultrasound of both breasts showed a 1.9 cm right retroareolar mass and an abnormal right axillary node; the left breast and axilla were normal. Core biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER 95 percent, PR 80 percent, HER2 1+, Ki-67 15 percent, with a positive node. Bilateral mastectomy and right axillary dissection: 1.8 cm tumor, margins clear, 1 of 14 nodes involved (4 mm, no extranodal extension), pT1c pN1a. No chemotherapy or radiation was given. Tamoxifen 20 mg daily since four weeks after surgery, with mild hot flashes. No germline testing yet. No history of blood clots, stroke, or liver disease. Never smoker; no alcohol. assessment.assessment: Breast cancer in men is less common than in women but is biologically similar, and most cases are hormone receptor-positive, as his is. With one small nodal metastasis, a strongly ER-positive grade 2 tumor, and his age of 83, endocrine therapy gives most of the benefit. The added gain from chemotherapy would be small and its harms greater at his age. Radiation after mastectomy for one involved node is a choice with a small gain in local control; with clear margins and no extranodal spread, omitting it is reasonable, and I agree with the decision made after surgery. No staging scans are needed without symptoms

Tamoxifen is the preferred adjuvant endocrine therapy for men. An aromatase inhibitor alone does not suppress estrogen adequately in men and is not recommended; it would be used only with a GnRH agonist if tamoxifen could not be taken. His mild hot flashes are common in men on tamoxifen. The main serious risk at his age is venous thromboembolism; he has no history of clots

Genetic counseling and germline testing should be offered to every man with breast cancer, whatever his age or family history. BRCA2 is the gene most often involved; a pathogenic variant would raise his risk of prostate and pancreatic cancer and would mean his relatives should be offered testing

Low bone mass at the femoral neck with mild vitamin D insufficiency. His fracture risk does not call for a bone drug. Bone-modifying drugs should not be given to prevent recurrence of early breast cancer in men, but can be used if osteoporosis develops

recommendations: Continue tamoxifen 20 mg daily for an initial five years; at five years, if he tolerates it, discuss five more years given the involved node. Do not switch to an aromatase inhibitor alone
No chemotherapy and no radiation now

Genetic counseling and a germline multigene panel (BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, and others), sent today; if a variant is found, a letter for relatives offering them testing, and prostate and pancreatic screening for him

Tamoxifen safety at each visit: symptoms of leg or lung clots, mood, hot flashes, sexual side effects such as lower libido or erectile problems, and adherence; avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine, and bupropion, which block its activation; report any change in vision

Surveillance: history and examination of both sides of the chest wall and both axillae every 3 to 6 months for 3 years, then every 6 to 12 months to 5 years, then yearly. No mammography, because both breasts were removed, and no routine blood tests, tumor markers, or scans without symptoms
Bone health: vitamin D 1000 units daily with a recheck in three months, calcium from food, weight-bearing exercise, and DXA every two years
Lymphedema risk reduction for the right arm and a written survivorship care plan within the first year
